title: POC scoping — workload geometry, token skew and latency SLOs (EquinoxHealth)
summary: Intro POC scoping focused on defining success criteria, deriving QPS/concurrency targets from real traffic, token input/output distributions, benchmark design (playback + synthetic), and timeline for a 6-week pilot. Security requirements (SOC2, SSO, KMS) and preference for initial dedicated pilot discussed.
topics: Token distribution (input vs output) and implications for cost/latency
Benchmark methodology: replay vs synthetic traces
action_items: Alex Mercer -> send benchmark template + sample CSV of request traces by 2026-03-17
Priya Sharma -> share 7 days of anonymized request logs (timestamps, prompt length, response length) by 2026-03-19
Dana Liu -> draft recommended concurrency/batching config for initial dedicated pool by 2026-03-20
Lina Gomez -> confirm SOC2 attestation doc access and list of compliance questions by 2026-03-18
next_steps: Redwood to run a quick replay estimate once EquinoxHealth shares trace CSV
Schedule 90-min deep-dive (SE-led) to finalize benchmark metrics and tooling (provision replay infra) — target 2026-03-22
Redwood to propose pilot pricing and capacity commit options after traffic analysis

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration approx: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood), Dana Liu (Redwood SE), Rohit Patel (Redwood Solutions), Michael Torres (EquinoxHealth Eng Mgr), Priya Sharma (Platform Eng), Jared Kim (SRE), Lina Gomez (Security)

Summary (auto): quick intro, then dive into traffic shape and success criteria. Action items captured.

[00:00] Alex Mercer: hey everybody, thanks for joining, uh, we'll run through what we need to scope a short pilot, focusing on the workload geometry and benchmark plan. Michael, do you want to kick with a little context about what success looks like for Equinox?

[00:20] Michael Torres: yeah sure, um thanks Alex. So the team's goal is to roll out a clinical triage assistant for virtual intake, initially to a subset of clinics. Success for us is twofold: p99 response under 800ms for short queries and overall cost per thousand prompts that keeps the feature within our product margins. We also care about token leakage — like ensuring PHI isn't stored outside our VPC.

[00:45] Priya Sharma: right and to add to that, our traffic has a pretty wide token distribution. We see a lot of short checks — like 8 to 20 input tokens with 30 to 60 outputs — but there are bursts where a clinician pastes long notes, 1k+ tokens, and that affects tail latency.

[01:10] Dana Liu: okay that's helpful. So two dims: the steady-state QPS and those long-tail heavy requests. For the POC we usually ask for a week of request traces with timestamps and lengths so we can build a QPS-concurrency model and run a replay.

[01:35] Jared Kim: we can provide anonymized logs, but to be clear we can't send raw PHI. We'll strip PII and only give token counts and timing.

[01:50] Lina Gomez: and security wise we need to validate your SOC2 Type II and KMS integration. We prefer the pilot in a VPC/private deployment, but if hosted can guarantee no retention and customer-managed keys, we might consider it for speed.

[02:15] Rohit Patel: understood. We support Private (VPC) deployments and Dedicated clusters. For quick turnaround we can run a hosted sandbox with customer-managed keys to run initial benchmarks, then lift-and-shift to Dedicated or on-prem as needed. Also we'll share our SOC2 stack docs.

[02:40] Alex Mercer: ok good. Let's talk numbers — Priya, what does your average QPS look like today and what's your peak?

[02:52] Priya Sharma: average is 4.2 QPS across the fleet during clinic hours, but peak burst windows hit 180 QPS for a couple minutes — usually when multiple intake forms hit after shift changes. Concurrency on our app layer sits around 150 during those bursts. Remember, our requests are often short but we have, like Michael said, sporadic long responses.

[03:20] Dana Liu: 180 QPS peak with 150 concurrency is a good starting point. For modeling we need the per-request input token and output token distribution. If 90% are under 60 tokens output but 1% are >800 tokens that will dominate cost and tail latency.

[03:45] Michael Torres: yes exactly. Our contention is the tail. If the p99 rises to 2 seconds during those long-doc submissions, clinicians complain and adoption stalls. So we want to tune fallback policies — maybe route long docs to a cheaper quantized model or asynchronous workflows.

[04:10] Dana Liu: we've done that before — smart routing and auto-fallback to a quantized variant can keep latency SLOs while controlling cost. We'll propose an initial policy: synchronous route for outputs <= 512 tokens, async job for >512, and fallback to smaller model if latency approaches 1.2 seconds.

[04:40] Priya Sharma: curious how you estimate batching effects — we batch at the runtime level, right? If we batch too aggressively latency goes up.

[04:52] Rohit Patel: yeah the runtime does continuous batching with configurable max batch window and max batch size. For short queries, batching reduces per-token cost substantially. For clinical workloads you typically set low batch windows (like 8-12ms) to keep latency predictable, and increase batch size caps to handle bursts. We'll recommend values based on the QPS histogram.

[05:20] Michael Torres: can you also show how KV cache helps when users do multi-turn triage? We want to avoid recomputing context tokens.

[05:30] Dana Liu: absolutely — KV cache is a big win for multi-turn, reduces compute per request after first turn. In our benchmark harness we simulate multi-turn sessions and measure effective tokens-per-second improvements. We'll include that in the benchmark plan.

[05:50] Jared Kim: on replay — do you replay against your hosted runtime or provide a local runner? We need to ensure replay doesn't hit prod data plane.

[06:02] Rohit Patel: good call. We run replays in a sandbox environment matching target capacity with identical runtime configs. For Private deployments we can also provide a local binary to run a replay on-prem, but usually customers opt for a Redwood sandbox to reduce setup time.

[06:25] Alex Mercer: let's outline the benchmark methodology: 1) Data ingestion — anonymized CSV with timestamp, input_token_count, expected_output_token_count, session_id. 2) Traffic replay at scaled QPS (we run baseline, 3x burst, and synthetic long-doc flood). 3) Measure per-model p50/p95/p99/p999 latencies, cost per 1k prompts, and throughput. 4) Validate tail SLOs and routing behavior.

[06:55] Michael Torres: that sounds good. For the CSV we'll need to confirm fields; Priya and I will scrub the data. We also need to know what fields you need for multi-turn: previous_context_token_count maybe?

[07:15] Dana Liu: include session_id and context_length tokens if possible; otherwise we can approximate by grouping by user id. For privacy you can hash session IDs.

[07:30] Priya Sharma: one practical ask — during the replay can you annotate which requests would be routed to a quantized model? We want to see the cost delta.

[07:42] Rohit Patel: yes we can run replay scenarios with routing policies enabled and produce comparative cost/latency reports. We'll include a version that simulates a quantized fallback with model A (4-bit) and model B (8-bit) so you can see tradeoffs.

[08:05] Michael Torres: and what's your approach to caching for repeated prompts? We have templated prompts that repeat at shift start — if cache hits we should see big savings.

[08:18] Dana Liu: our prefix caching detects exact prompt matches and we keep a TTL; we can also do fuzzy-match caching for templated prompts which gives partial token savings. We'll include cache hit rate metrics in the report.

[08:36] Alex Mercer: switching to timeline — we're aiming for a 6-week pilot. Week 0 is data handoff and security signoff, Week 1-2 run replay + analytics, Week 3 tune configs and run baseline benchmarks, Week 4 run high-burst tests and routing validation, Week 5 run customer acceptance tests, Week 6 wrap and recommend production capacity. Thoughts?

[09:05] Priya Sharma: that seems reasonable. We do want to compress if possible — if the security review is quick we can shorten to 4 weeks by overlapping staging and replay.

[09:20] Lina Gomez: security gating items: SOC2 report, vendor penetration test summary, SSO/SAML integration flow, KMS usage, data retention policy. We'll need the SOC2 artifact and a security questionnaire.

[09:40] Rohit Patel: we'll push the SOC2 Type II report and a filled-in security questionnaire today. We also support bringing our runtime into your VPC for the private pilot if you prefer.

[09:58] Michael Torres: pricing model question — for POC do you charge per token or is there a trial credit for benchmarking?

[10:08] Alex Mercer: we typically offer an eval credit for the pilot covering baseline runs; post-eval there are usage charges. For Dedicated pilots we discuss a short-term capacity commit — we'll send options.

[10:22] Priya Sharma: about latency SLOs, you mentioned p999 earlier. For us p99 is critical, but p999 is also important during hourly audits — what's realistic?

[10:35] Dana Liu: p999 is sensitive to outliers like OS preemption or long-doc requests. With a tuned dedicated pool and pre-warmed instances you can often achieve p99 ~ 600-800ms and p999 ~ 2s for mixed workloads, but this depends on token length distribution and concurrency. We'll model exact numbers from your traces.

[10:58] Jared Kim: do you have any recommended throttling or backpressure patterns for clients when the service is momentarily overloaded? We prefer graceful degradation.

[11:10] Rohit Patel: yes common patterns: 1) client-side queuing with circuit-breaker, 2) response size limit and async fallback for big docs, 3) model-routing to cheaper variants, 4) cache-first responses for templated content. We'll detail recommended configs.

[11:30] Michael Torres: ok let's capture the specific success criteria. From product side: 1) p99 <800ms for synchronous triage flows under peak expected load (180 QPS). 2) cost per 1k prompts under $X (we'll put placeholder until we get model mix). 3) zero outward PHI leakage and KMS-controlled keys. Are we aligned?

[11:55] Alex Mercer: yes aligned. We'll also add an operational success metric: automated failover and templates for routing rollback with less than 10 minutes to restore baseline behavior.

[12:10] Priya Sharma: what's the instrumentation? We need token-level metrics, per-route latency, and per-model cost split.

[12:22] Dana Liu: our Console exposes per-route token breakdowns, cost attribution, latency percentiles, and tracing hooks. We'll give you a demo of the Console in the SE deep-dive.

[12:38] Michael Torres: fine. A couple quick gotchas: our infra enforces strict egress rules — if you run a hosted sandbox we need to ensure IP allowlists etc. Also we may need a short NDA addendum for the POC logs.

[12:56] Alex Mercer: we can provide allowlist IPs and sign a narrow NDA addendum for replay logs. We'll loop legal.

[13:10] Rohit Patel: action item recap: we'll share benchmark template CSV and SOC2 docs. We will also draft an initial routing/batching config and a replay cost estimate once you hand over traces.

[13:30] Michael Torres: Priya and I will scrub and send logs by Thu (2026-03-19). Lina will send security questionnaire items.

[13:40] Alex Mercer: great. Any final questions?

[13:45] Priya Sharma: one more — do you support model quantization parameters per-customer? Like certain quant levels only for private deployments?

[13:55] Dana Liu: yes we can restrict model variants by deployment. For compliance reasons some customers prefer 8-bit only for on-prem. We'll document options.

[14:10] Michael Torres: ok thanks everyone. Looking forward to the SE deep-dive and the replay.

[14:20] Alex Mercer: thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites and send the template. End meeting.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-hears present (e.g., "KV cache" transcribed correctly but some product names like "Redwood Dedicated" may appear as "Redwood dedicate" or "Redwood dedikate"), filler words present, timestamps approximate to speaker segments.
